cues.text: In 1640, during the civil war that divided Piedmont, the French army of the Count d'Harcourt crossed the Po River and advanced on Turin, Italy, overrunning the Savoyard defenses along the way.

Soldiers reached the hilltop church of Santa Maria del Monte, home to a community of Capuchin friars, and broke in, killing many civilians who had taken refuge inside — though the friars themselves were spared.
Amid the violence, a French soldier succeeded in forcing open the tabernacle and seizing the pyx that held the consecrated Hosts inside.
At the instant he took hold of it, witnesses reported that something like a line of fire burst from the tabernacle and struck him directly, burning his face and clothing.
The soldier, badly burned, dropped what he had taken.
The second episode in Turin's history to bear the name Eucharistic miracle followed the far more celebrated 1453 event at Corpus Domini.
It became known locally simply as the miracle of the Monte, tied to the church that still stands above the city and the river.
Together, the events of 1453 and 1640 came to form what local tradition calls Turin's Eucharistic itinerary.
These two episodes, nearly two centuries apart, both centered on consecrated Hosts resisting improper or violent handling in the city's own streets and churches.
Both remain marked by their respective sanctuaries today.

The church of Santa Maria del Monte dei Cappuccini still overlooks Turin and the Po from its hilltop position, carrying the memory of 1640 alongside the older and better-documented account from Corpus Domini across the city below.
The 1453 miracle turned on a mule's collapse in a public square.
The 1640 account turns on wartime desecration met, in the telling, by fire answering fire—a soldier's violence turned back on the hand that offered it.
